items.title: Outraging modesty provision under BNS applies to transgender women: Bombay High Court
items.summary: The Nagpur Bench of the Bombay High Court has ruled that a transgender person who identifies as a woman can also invoke legal provisions meant to protect a woman's modesty under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) [Vishal Sunil Ingle v. State of Maharashtra]. Justice Mehroz K Pathan on November 3, 2026 dismissed a criminal revision application filed by the accused, Vishal Sunil Ingle. He had challenged the rejection of his discharge application. “The perusal of the FIR would show that the complainant/victim has identified herself to be a woman and the aforesaid self determination cannot be questioned at least at the present stage while accused is seeking discharge,” the judge said. Justice Mehroz K Pathan He concluded that “allegations of assault and outraging the modesty of a woman can be sustained even where the victim is a transgender person who identifies herself as a woman.” The accused, an Agniveer in the Indian Army, faced charges under Section 75 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and Section 18(D) of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019. The complainant alleged that the applicant committed sexual assault under a false promise of marriage in October 2025

items.title: Animal, Pushpa, KGF: When cinema turns violence into heroism | Let Me Explain 176 | Pooja Prasanna
items.summary: A 15-year-old girl was attacked with a chainsaw inside her classroom in Andhra Pradesh. The brutality of the attack shocked people across the country. After the initial shock, another conversation started. Many began pointing to films such as Animal, KGF and Pushpa, where extreme violence is presented as an expression of masculinity, anger and power. And then came a response from the overlord of alpha-male cinema, director Sandeep Reddy Vanga. He said that when a horrific crime takes place, the first response should be empathy for the victim. He accused critics of using the incident as an opportunity to target filmmakers and said cinema was being made a scapegoat. Watching a movie with violence alone does not automatically make someone violent. There is little evidence to establish such a direct cause-and-effect relationship. But that is also a rather simplistic way of looking at the criticism.Because the question is not just whether films make people violent.
